chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated to us from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Abdullah ibn Talha al-Nahdi, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his forefathers (peace be upon them). He said: The Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family) said:

Four are those whose supplication is never rejected, and for whose supplication the gates of heaven are opened and it reaches the Throne: the supplication of the parent for his child, the supplication of the oppressed against his oppressor, the supplication of the pilgrim until he returns, and the supplication of the fasting person until he breaks his fast.

key_terms.الصائم: The fasting person — one observing sawm (fasting)
key_terms.العرش: The Throne (al-'Arsh) — the divine Throne of God, representing the highest realm
key_terms.المعتمر: One performing Umrah — the lesser pilgrimage to Mecca
key_terms.دعوة: Supplication (du'a) — a prayer or invocation to God

ai.seo_question: Whose supplications are never rejected according to Prophet Muhammad?
ai.summary: The Prophet Muhammad (SAWW), through a chain going back via the Imams, identifies four categories of people whose supplications are guaranteed acceptance by God and ascend directly to the Divine Throne. This hadith was narrated in the assembly of al-Saduq in Safar 368 AH, reflecting the importance early Shia scholars placed on the spiritual efficacy of du'a in specific states of devotion and vulnerability.

en.bilal-muhammad: Muhammad b. al-Hasan b. Ahmad b. al-Walid (ra) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad b. al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated to us from Muhammad b. al-Husayn b. Abi’l Khattab from `Ali b. al-Nu`man from `Abdullah b. Talha al-Nahdi from Ja`far b. Muhammad from his father from his forefathers (as). He said: The Messenger of Allah (s) said:

The gates of heaven open up to the supplications of four, which go straight to the Throne: (1) the supplication of the parent for his child, (2) that of the oppressed against his oppressor, (3) that of the pilgrim until he returns, and (4) that of the fasting person until he breaks his fast.
